chokhmat_shlomo.en: Seif 1: There is no karet liability except for melacha, eating, and drinking. In my opinion: see Magen Avraham who wrote nevertheless all are d'oraisa. In truth this law is not agreed — Rosh and Ran hold only rabbinic. I examined Ran — his proof is from permitting children to wash and feed them, and it says "you shall not eat, you shall not feed them" to warn adults regarding minors, end of his words. In my opinion this does not follow — perhaps the Torah warned only regarding something that is an actual negative prohibition, not regarding what is only a positive commandment, for punishment and warning certainly do not apply here except violating the positive "afflict your souls"; if so there is no proof from this except like running which is a negative prohibition. Also one may distinguish for a minor female — this is a positive time-bound commandment from which women are exempt; we only learn from "man or woman" who were equated to all Torah punishments, and this fits where there is punishment and warning, but where there is no punishment and warning one may say women are exempt; therefore one may say for women these afflictions are rabbinic, therefore an adult may anoint a minor girl — for women it is only rabbinic but for males from the Torah. So it appears at first glance. But apart from this and apart from this, we may ask: the Torah did not say "you shall not eat, you shall not feed them" except regarding a matter where the minor's act is also considered an act — such as eating, for is a minor's eating not eating? It is eating, only he is exempt from commandments; so too entering a tent for a corpse — a minor has an act and entering a tent is considered real entry, only the minor is exempt and the adult may not do so for him. But on Yom Kippur it is not written "eating" but "affliction," and in affliction one may say the matter is contingent on settling the mind; since we hold a minor lacks daat, his eating is not settling the mind, and all the more so his other pleasures are not settling the mind — there is no prohibited act at all, unlike all prohibitions where the act is a prohibited act and only the minor is exempt from commandments. On Yom Kippur where the matter is contingent on settling the mind, since a minor's mind is not considered mind there is no prohibited act; and if an adult ate without his mind settling he is exempt from the Torah, and though forbidden it is only from chazi le'itztareif — this does not apply to a minor, examine and inquire. Ran's words there are unclear to me — according to his words how answer food permitted to feed a minor as explicit in the Mishna, and eating is certainly from the Torah with karet? It seems Ran sensed this and concealed it in soft language: "these are certainly for pleasure, and if withheld one day they are not endangered," etc. — implying eating is different because withholding endangers. But difficult: if only due to danger they should give less than a shiur like a dangerously ill person — why give full shiur? Cannot say they only give less than shiur — below we say Shammai the Elder had them feed with both hands from old age, and Ran agreed to Rashi that even if he washed hands in the morning he must wash again for eating. Perforce it discusses full shiur — for less than shiur why require netilat yadayim, we never heard one must wash for an infant less than shiur; perforce full shiur, and netilat yadayim discusses egg-size while Yom Kippur shiur is less than an egg — proven they feed full shiur and more; if only danger permitted why better than dangerous patient? Perforce not from danger, perforce another reason as above, examine. Ran's words require study. See Beit Yosef who brought two views whether afflictions besides eating and drinking are d'oraisa or rabbinic. I saw Beer Sheva in Keritut plainly rabbinic — wondrous how he did not notice many views, especially as Levush student and Levush says d'oraisa. Also wondrous Beit Yosef did not bring Rashi Yoma "Shabbaton Shabbaton" implying d'oraisa by comparing to Shabbat melacha tolados not in Mishkan which are d'oraisa. Initially I thought this is contingent on R' Yosef and R' Elazar — Mishna groups Yom Kippur forbidden in eating etc.; for R' Yosef chatzi shiur forbidden d'oraisa, since eating intention is d'oraisa so too others d'oraisa — how split "forbidden" for two parts? For R' Elazar chatzi shiur rabbinic, since eating only rabbinic so too washing rabbinic. But I have compelling proof d'oraisa from Gemara: when it teaches "forbidden" it refers to the rest — Rabba and R' Yosef in other books of the yeshiva: whence Yom Kippur forbidden? Scripture teaches "Shabbaton Shabbaton," end of his words. That "Rabba taught" is incomprehensible — why need this generality, Mishna explicit these are forbidden? I saw Kefot Temarim: proof these fit language of prohibition — wondrous: why need proof, Mishna proves even if "forbidden" also on eating it still applies to them; and since forbidden why not fit "forbidden," unless thought rabbinic lacks "forbidden"? Answer one: many rabbinic prohibitions use "forbidden," and after them in Taanit "forbidden in eating and drinking," and Pesachim ch. 4 Beit Shammai forbid and Beit Hillel are stringent. Also this proof should have been brought above when answering R' Elazar — why not first? Rather Gemara intends proof per second explanation: "forbidden" refers to the rest without the first answer that R' Elazar admits rabbinic — if so these too rabbinic, yet "Rabba and R' Yosef taught Shabbaton Shabbaton" proves d'oraisa. If so how think Mishna teaches "forbidden" on eating meaning chatzi shiur rabbinic while others d'oraisa — how split "forbidden" with a sharp knife? Perforce only on the rest, d'oraisa — clear proof in my opinion. Also without Rashi "when it teaches forbidden the rest," one could say it refers to the braita "although Sages said forbidden in all" from which Gemara asked above — answer: when braita teaches "forbidden in all" it means the rest without karet. But difficult: "Sages said" implies d'oraisa, else should say "although Sages enacted" or "decreed"; "Sages said" implies only speech of Sages but law d'oraisa; therefore "when it teaches forbidden the rest" meaning Rabba taught proves d'oraisa, hence "Sages said" fits — examine. First way seems more correct. Per above understand Gemara "Rabba and R' Yosef in other books" — Rashi: not here only "He spoke and Mishneh Torah" — incomprehensible what difference where taught; certainly no empty words in Gemara; examine Yoma ch. 1 p. 81 and Tanna brings from here, R' Acha bar Yaakov learns Shabbat Shabbaton from Shabbat Bereishit until Tanna of "that bone on the ninth of the month what does it do," etc. — proven Tanna of bone learns warning from there and other amoraim learn elsewhere, perforce not like bone Tanna; that Tanna is Sifra — if braita taught washing etc. d'oraisa should teach in Sifra; possible he holds warning from bone and remaining Shabbaton for other afflictions; but others not learning bone hold like R' Acha bar Yaakov warning from Shabbat Shabbaton, perforce mufneh else challenge Shabbat more severe stoning, perforce mufneh — cannot learn more; therefore only rabbinic, hence Gemara says they learned in other books not bone Tanna, yet learned prohibition of these afflictions, perforce other amoraim learned warnings elsewhere, therefore all d'oraisa, perforce "forbidden" on other matters for R' Elazar not chatzi shiur rabbinic — examine well, correct with the Omnipresent's help. I already wrote wondrous Beit Yosef did not bring Rashi Yoma "the rest" implying rabbinic; Rambam from Mishna implies d'oraisa per his rulings. Initially seemed rabbinic — else how R' Eliezer permits king and bride? I saw Beit Yosef citing rishonim this proof; else why Gemara proof from other books not in karet — should prove from Mishna permitting R' Eliezer king and bride proves rabbinic; for unambiguous term used only "forbidden." Cannot say no proof from Mishna — perhaps Sages who forbade hold d'oraisa and dispute whether d'oraisa or rabbinic — R' Eliezer rabbinic, Sages d'oraisa; hence proof from other books rabbinic per Rashi: else what proof from other books, perhaps R' Eliezer and not Sages — requires study. There I saw Rashi beginning of chapter "chatzi shiur" meaning less than shiur forbidden d'oraisa below derives from "kol chelev" — wondrous why Rashi here; seems resolves Pri Megadim doubt ch. 1 chametz umatzah whether Torah "eating" is kol shehu only liability kezayit or Torah eating is kezayit. Rashi holds Torah eating is kol shehu, liability kezayit — hence Rashi's difficulty: in all prohibitions chatzi shiur forbidden d'oraisa from chazi le'itztareif — truly eating is kol shehu, so less or full shiur is eating, liability kezayit, chazi le'itztareif helps; on Yom Kippur affliction is contingent on mind — less than shiur no settling mind, no chazi le'itztareif, as if not eaten yet liable as if ate — no chazi le'itztareif; therefore Rashi primary reason chatzi shiur d'oraisa not chazi le'itztareif but learn from kol chelev, no distinction Yom Kippur; R' Yochanan who said reason chazi le'itztareif holds like those who derive reason of verse. Gemara establishes Mishna like chatzi shiur like those not deriving reason — since learn kol chelev, also Yom Kippur — examine. This resolves Gemara returning "works for R' Yochanan not R' Elazar" — we already asked in our novellae there; per above: R' Yochanan said reason chazi le'itztareif yet learn kol chelev — either derives reason like R' Shimon or intention: since truly Sages do not derive all, only where reason plausible derive kol as Tosafot — R' Yochanan since reason chazi le'itztareif plausible, derive kol; but now derive kol, no longer derive reason to forbid without chazi le'itztareif — Gemara doubts R' Yochanan's intent. First: if R' Yochanan like R' Shimon derives reason, Mishna should not work for him only for us — Mishna chatzi shiur, not R' Yochanan since he like R' Shimon derives reason and R' Yochanan holds halacha like stam mishna, stam like R' Yosef not deriving reason, forbids Yom Kippur too — for us Mishna works not R' Yochanan. Then: if R' Yochanan also not derive reason and chazi le'itztareif only why derive kol — since derive kol proves not derive reason, also R' Yochanan Mishna works — hence "works for R' Yochanan," hence doubled language of doubt — examine with the Omnipresent's help. Per above resolves Pri Megadim doubt Yoreh Deah gid hanasheh whether chatzi shiur d'oraisa applies — no chazi le'itztareif; per truth we hold not derive reason, learn kol chelev everywhere chatzi shiur; R' Yochanan who gave chazi le'itztareif reason intended as above — so in my opinion.

(א) (a) Eliaso as his name - dictates west until evening:

peri_megadim.he: והתירו עט״ז רש״י שבת קי״ד וקט״ו עגמת נפש ממנחה ולמעלה ששואף ומצפה ללילה לאכילה ואין אוכל הוי עינוי טפי הא קודם מנחה אין עגמת נפש דיודע שיש עדין זמן רב עד אכילה לא התירו דשבות הוא לתקן לצורך חול ומ״ש הט״ז דלא הוי שינוי כו׳ כוונתו כפירש״י בהא דמחרפי וכאמור והר״ן ומ״מ פירשו עגמת נפש דאדרבא התירו לתקן שלא יהא עגומה וימצא מזון ביד במוצאי יוה״כ ונ״מ בהטמנת חמין בתר״י להר׳ן ומ״מ שרי שלא יהא־ עגומה ולרש״י י״ל דאסור. ומנחה למעלה יש לעיין או מנחה גדולה או קטנה קאמר והאידנא נהגו לאסור. ועמ״ש אי״ה באות ב׳:
peri_megadim.en: And they permitted — Taz: Rashi Shabbat 114 and 115 — distress from minchah anticipating night eating; they did not permit before minchah as no distress yet; forbidden as preparing weekday need. Taz: not change, etc., means per Rashi; Ran and Maharam: permitted to repair so not distressed and food ready at motzaei — unlike Rashi; when Yom Kippur erev Shabbat permitted insulating so not distressed — per Ran; per Rashi forbidden. See Pri Megadim letter 2.

turei_zahav.he: והתירו לקנב ירק. פירש"י לנתק העלין מהקלחי' כדי להשות' שיהיו מוכנים לחתכן ושרי משו' דהוי עינוי שרואה מזומן ואינו אוכל עכ"ל והר"ן והמ"מ פ"א מהל' שבית' עשור פי' משום עגמת נפש כדי שתהא קל למזון והוה כמו שיש לו פת בסלו ומדברי הטור סי' תר"ט משמע שמפרש כפי' השני דאלו לפירש"י לא מקשה הטור מידי שם על הטמנת חמין לפירש"י הא דאסור קודם מנחה משום דלא הוי אז שינוי ואסור משום שבות:
turei_zahav.en: And they permitted trimming vegetables. Rashi: to detach leaves from stalks so they are ready to cut — permitted because of affliction, seeing prepared food and not eating, end of his words; Ran and Magen Avraham ch. 1 laws of Shabbat explain due to distress so food is easy at mealtime, like having bread in one's basket; from Tur siman 249 it appears second explanation — if per Rashi why question there on insulating hot food? Rather per second explanation only from minchah onward when affliction is greater; before minchah not permitted as not yet affliction and forbidden as preparing for weekday need.

yad_ephraim.en: In the 16th section 1 for the food for the evening and precisely after the minachah, as it is, there is no such thing as torture, 21 and 2 of the 1st section of the Gemara:

mechaber.he: כל מלאכה שחייבים עליה בשבת חייבים עליה ביום הכפורים וכל שבשבת פטור אבל אסור גם ביום הכפורים כן אלא שבשבת זדונו בסקילה ויום הכפורים זדונו בכרת וכל שאסור לטלטלו בשבת אסור לטלטלו ביום הכפורים והתירו לקנב ירק ולפצוע אגוזים מן המנחה ולמעלה כשחל בחול והאידנא נהגו לאסור: הגה אם נפלה דליקה ביה"כ מותר להציל סעודה אחת לצורך לילה כמו שמציל בשבת לסעודת מנחה (ר"ן פרק כל כתבי) וכבר נתבאר סימן של"ד כיצד נוהגים בזמן הזה בדליקה בשבת וה"ה ביוה"כ ונהגו שהתינוקות משחקים באגוזים (אגודה ומהרי"ל) ואין למחות בידם אפי' קודם מנחה ונשתרבב המנהג מדין הפצעת אגוזים הנזכר (ד"ע):
mechaber.en: Every melachah for which one is liable on Shabbos, one is liable for it on Yom Kippur; and whatever on Shabbos is exempt but forbidden is likewise [exempt but forbidden] on Yom Kippur — except that on Shabbos its deliberate [violation] is [punishable] by stoning, and on Yom Kippur its deliberate [violation] is by kares. And whatever is forbidden to handle on Shabbos is forbidden to handle on Yom Kippur. And they permitted to trim vegetables and to crack nuts from Minchah-time onward when it falls on a weekday; but nowadays the custom is to forbid. {Rama: If a fire broke out on Yom Kippur, it is permitted to save one meal for the need of the night, just as one saves on Shabbos for the Minchah meal (Ran, chapter "Kol Kisvei"). And it has already been explained in siman 334 how we act nowadays regarding a fire on Shabbos, and the same applies on Yom Kippur. And the custom is that children play with nuts (Agudah; Maharil), and one should not protest against them, even before Minchah; and the custom evolved from the law of cracking nuts mentioned (his own opinion).}
